"executive_summary": "This study investigated whether the length of a chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion influences angiographic and clinical outcomes after successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive patients who underwent successful CTO PCI with DES between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30mm, n=76). Baseline characteristics were largely similar, with prior PCI more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions more frequent in the short CTO group. In-hospital complications were comparable except for a higher incidence of significant intimal dissection in the long CTO group. At six months, angiographic outcomes were similar between the two groups, including binary restenosis, in-stent restenosis, and late loss, although there was a numerically higher trend toward binary restenosis in the long CTO group (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12). Over two years, the incidence of total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), myocardial infarction (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71), and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13) did not differ significantly between the groups. However, the incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05) and target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05) was significantly higher in the long CTO group. Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52-11.8, p<0.05). The authors concluded that, despite successful CTO PCI with DES, long CTO lesions are associated with a higher rate of repeat revascularization, though this did not translate into differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The study acknowledges limitations including its non-randomized, single-center design, relatively small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and insufficient follow-up duration. These findings suggest that while long CTO lesions carry a higher risk of repeat revascularization, the overall safety and long-term clinical outcomes remain comparable to those of short CTO lesions, supporting the notion that procedural success with DES does not guarantee improved outcomes in long CTO disease. summary.title: Impact of Chronic Total Occlusion Lesion Length on Six-month Angiographic and 2-year Clinical Outcomes
summary.authors: Jihun Ahn; Byounggeol Choi; Yeon Choi; Jae Kyeong Byun; Ahmed Mashaly; Kareem Abdelshafi; Yoonjee Park; Young Jang; Woohyeun Kim; Eunjin Park; Jin Oh Na; Cheol Ung Choi; Eungju Kim; Chang Gyu Park; Hongseog Seo; Dongjoo Oh; Jinsu Byeon; Sangho Park; Hyeyon Yu; Seung-Woon W Rha
summary.executive_summary: This study investigated whether the length of a chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion influences angiographic and clinical outcomes after successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive patients who underwent successful CTO PCI with DES between November 2004 and October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (angiographic lesion length <30mm, n=76). Baseline characteristics were largely similar, with prior PCI more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions more frequent in the short CTO group. In-hospital complications were comparable except for a higher incidence of significant intimal dissection in the long CTO group. At six months, angiographic outcomes were similar between the two groups, including binary restenosis, in-stent restenosis, and late loss, although there was a numerically higher trend toward binary restenosis in the long CTO group (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12). Over two years, the incidence of total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), myocardial infarction (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71), and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13) did not differ significantly between the groups. However, the incidence of repeat PCI (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05) and target vessel revascularization (TVR) (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05) was significantly higher in the long CTO group. Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53-11.9, p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52-11.8, p<0.05). The authors concluded that, despite successful CTO PCI with DES, long CTO lesions are associated with a higher rate of repeat revascularization, though this did not translate into differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The study acknowledges limitations including its non-randomized, single-center design, relatively small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and insufficient follow-up duration. These findings suggest that while long CTO lesions carry a higher risk of repeat revascularization, the overall safety and long-term clinical outcomes remain comparable to those of short CTO lesions, supporting the notion that procedural success with DES does not guarantee improved outcomes in long CTO disease. The authors emphasize the need for larger, long-term studies to draw definitive conclusions. This work contributes to the understanding of lesion-length-specific outcomes in the DES era and highlights the importance of considering baseline lesion characteristics when predicting clinical outcomes after CTO PCI. The results have implications for patient counseling, procedural planning, and the potential need for more aggressive surveillance or intervention strategies in patients with long CTO lesions. Overall, the study provides valuable insights into the nuanced relationship between CTO lesion length and clinical outcomes, while acknowledging the limitations of its observational design and the need for further research to confirm its findings. Research Context
Drug-eluting stents have reduced restenosis and adverse events after PCI. Long coronary lesions remain a worse prognostic factor after PCI. CTO PCI success rates remain lower than non-CTO PCI. Long-term CTO outcomes depend on clinical risk factors and baseline lesion characteristics. No definitive answers exist for CTO outcomes according to lesion length in the DES era.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate whether CTO lesion length impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes. The authors hypothesized that adverse clinical and angiographic outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. Long CTO lesions were expected to have worse clinical risk factors such as prior MI and PCI. Newer-generation DES use was expected to be more common in the short CTO group. Long CTO was predicted to be an independent predictor of repeat PCI.

Methodological Details
The study enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients who underwent successful PCI with DES. Patients were enrolled from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital. Patients were divided into long CTO (≥30mm) and short CTO (<30mm) groups. The long CTO group comprised 159 patients and the short CTO group comprised 76 patients. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study. CTO was defined as complete obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0 and duration ≥3 months. Only de novo lesions were included, and CTO due to in-stent restenosis was excluded. Loading doses of clopidogrel (300-600mg) and aspirin (200-300mg) were administered before the procedure. Maintenance therapy included aspirin (100mg) and clopidogrel (75mg) as dual antiplatelet therapy. Clopidogrel was encouraged to continue for at least one year. Cilostazol was administered by 200mg post-loading and then 100mg twice a day for at least one month.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI procedures were performed using current guidelines with standard techniques. Various guidewires were used to cross the CTO lesion. Atheroablative devices were not utilized; simple balloon pre-dilation was mostly performed. All PCI was performed using DES, with stent type decided by the operator. Procedural success was defined as final diameter stenosis <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. QCA parameters were measured before PCI, immediately after PCI, and 6 months after the procedure. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included ISR, mean DS, MLD, and late loss at 6 months. Follow-up data were collected at two years via interview, medical record review, and/or telephone contact. The primary clinical endpoint was MACE, defined as total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization. Secondary clinical endpoints included death, MI, repeat PCI, TLR, TVR, and non-TVR. Continuous variables were analyzed with Student's t-test, and categorical variables with χ2 or Fisher's exact test.

Key Results
The long CTO group comprised 159 patients and the short CTO group comprised 76 patients. Prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group. Bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. In-hospital complications were similar between the two groups except for intimal dissection. Six-month angiographic outcomes were similar between the two groups. The incidence of binary restenosis was 19.1% vs. 8.8% (p=0.12) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of ISR was 33.3% vs. 26.6% (p=0.42) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm vs. 0.46 ± 0.56 mm (p=0.13) between the long and short CTO groups. Total death was 3.1% vs. 5.2% (p=0.43) between the long and short CTO groups. Cardiac death was 1.2% vs. 2.6% (p=0.45) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of MI was 1.8% vs. 2.6% (p=0.71) between the long and short CTO groups.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Long CTO lesions carry worse clinical risk factors such as prior MI and PCI. The higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR in the long CTO group did not translate into differences in hard endpoints. The presence of less myocardial viability and collateral channels may lessen the harmful effects of restenosis. Long CTO was an independent predictor of repeat PCI with an OR of 4.26. Long CTO was an independent predictor of TVR with an OR of 4.23.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is not a randomized study and is a single-center registry. Baseline clinical, lesion, and procedural characteristics were slightly different between the two groups. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. The sample size was relatively small, limiting the power to detect differences in angiographic events. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy.

Claims
Long CTO lesions are associated with a higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR, but not with differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The incidence of repeat PCI was 18.8% vs. 7.8% (p<0.05) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of TVR was 16.3% vs. 6.5% (p<0.05) between the long and short CTO groups. Long CTO was an independent predictor of repeat PCI with an OR of 4.26. Long CTO was an independent predictor of TVR with an OR of 4.23. Total death was 3.1% vs. 5.2% (p=0.43) between the long and short CTO groups. Cardiac death was 1.2% vs. 2.6% (p=0.45) between the long and short CTO groups. The incidence of MACE was 21.3% vs. 13.1% (p=0.13) between the long and short CTO groups. The higher incidence of TVR in the long CTO group did not translate into differences in hard endpoints. PCI in the long CTO lesion with DES is similarly safe as compared with CTO PCI in the short CTO lesion. Long-term studies with larger populations are needed to draw definitive conclusions.
Successful CTO PCI with DES is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with failed CTO PCI, including reduced rates of CABG. Successful CTO PCI was associated with reduced rates of CABG compared with failed CTO PCI. The incidence of MACE was 21.3% vs. 13.1% (p=0.13) between the long and short CTO groups. The safety profile, mid-term angiographic and long-term clinical outcomes were similar between the long CTO and the short CTO group.

Data And Code Availability
The study data were collected prospectively from a single-center registry.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used strict statistical adjustment for risk factors such as sex, age, hypertension, DM, CKD, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. There could be unmeasured confounders and analytical bias despite strict statistical adjustment.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.

Three Takeaways
The core contribution is that long CTO lesions are associated with a higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR, but not with differences in hard clinical endpoints. The strongest evidence is the multivariate analysis showing long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26) and TVR (OR 4.23). The future path is to conduct long-term studies with larger populations to draw definitive conclusions.
